the Atlantic Coast, sinking a
dozen or more Allied and neu-
tral vessels.

name, ''cantaloupe," from the Castle of

melon from Armenia was cultivated for
the first time.

seed to the new world on his second
voyage, where Il quickly spread to both

REHOBOTH BEACH, Del,
Aug. 20.-The combination Of
calm seas and warm weather
found along the Delaware
coast in late August and early
September seemingly affects
fish and fishermen alike -
bringing out both in greater
numbers.


Currently, fish - in many
varieties and sizeS--are being
taken from Delaware's many
inland bays, and from the surf
line and depths of the Atlantic.
Included are founder. bluefish,
trout. mackerel, bonito. porgies.
sea bass. ling cod and tautog,
and even the more elusive mar
lin.


Charter boats, operating out
Of the Indian River Basin, have
recently been reporting marlin
catches with blue martins being
taken we'll out in the Atlantic
near the warmer Gulf Stream
waters and white martins being
boated closer to shore.


Less expensive and favored
by many of the fishermen who
come to this area in summer
and early fall is the offshore
bottom fishing done from what
are called bottom boats or
head boats"


These boats depart from the
Indian River Basin and other
nearby ports in the early morn
ing hours and are guided by ex-
perienced shippers to a pre-
determined location, where they
are then anchored. Anchorage
is generally over or near sunken
wrecks which attract the small
fish upon which the larger
porgies and sea bass feed.


In addition to offering rental
service on rods and reels, many
Of the bottom boats have snack
and beverage facilities and
some are even equipped with a
tiny lunch counter Offering
sandwiches, coffee, soft drinks
and even seasick pills.


While all the bottom boats
schedule early morning fishing
trips, it is not always necessary
for late sleeping anglers to miss
all the fun. Some afternoon
fishing trips are also scheduled.
! leaving the docks about l
o'clock in the afternoon.


Offshore bottom boat fishing
will likely experience even
greater popularity when two
artificial reefs, now under con-
struction. are completed and
placed in position. Composed
largely Of concrete pipe. these
reefs" are to be placed on the
ocean bottom near the Inlet in
the near future as part of an
effort to develop additional fish
feeding grounds in this area.

SAN FRANCISCO. Sept. 10
(AP). - The convict sitdowr
strike at Alcatraz Federal Pris-
on showed it's first break today
when "a kitchen and mess hall
workers offered to return to
their jobs.


Warden Paul Madigan said
they would be put to work
tomorrow, relieving guards who
have been handling the food
since the trouble started Mon.
day. The 260 prisoners affected
by the strike have been sub
sisting mainly on sandwiches
and water.

formal demand. Warden Madi-
gan said his investigation
showed they want newspapers
and commissary privileges en-
joyed in normal prisons.


Alcatraz, maximum security
prison in San Francisco Bay,
has been reserved for incor-
rigibles. Privileges have been
limited by the Federal Bureau
of Prisons.

SANTIAGO, Chile. Nov. /
(AP). - Three violent earth
quakes rocked Southern Chile
today, tumbling walls and buck
ling streets in half a dozen
cities. Men, women and chill
dren ran through the streets in
panic.


The earth rumblings, shortly
before dawn, were felt from
Conception on the southern
Pacific coast to Puerto Montt,
$50 miles further south in the
lake region.


Telephone and telegraph
communications were knocked
out but later were restored.


There were no immediate re-
ports Of any dead or injured
or any estimate of damage.


The shocks were the strong
est recorded since May 21-22
when all of Southern Chile was
devastated, with hundreds
killed and thousands injured.
Property damage then was esti-
mated at $3.50 million.


Some Of the buildings and
homes that survived the May
earthquakes were reported col
lapsed today.


Thousands Of Chileans at
tending early mass at Roman
Catholic churches throughout
the south, in observance of All
Saints Day, felt the quakes.


The Seismological Institute
said the series was q continual
tion Of normal after-shocks evi-
dent since May.

Among all the newly independent
nations, perhaps none has been born
In such complex of compromise as the
Republic Of Cyprus. After centuries of
foreign occupation and rule, this Medi-
terranean island opened new chapter
in It's history last week under interlock-
ing treaty relationships with Britain,
Greece and Turkey, with it's govern
mental structure shared on carefully
partitioned basis between Greek and
Turkish Cypriots and with its population
similarly divided in culture, politics and
economics.


With all the usual problems Of a
young and not self-sufficient nation,
plus others uniquely its own, its future
will depend upon collaboration as intri-
cate as was the compromise that gave
it birth. 1t is not surprising that the
hour of independence, the moment when
the British flag was lowered for the first
time in 88 years in the capital city of
Nicosia was greeted with reserve by
Greek and Turkish communities alike.


And yet there are real grounds for
hope in the craftsmanship demonstrated
by the two men who played the leading
roles in working out this unusual So
luton and who remain to implement it
President Makarios, the Greek Cypriot,
and Vice President Kutchuk the Turk
ish Cypriot. Each has strong public sup
port and each has directed it toward
accommodation in the common cause of
independence. In the light Of their
accomplishments in the recent past, the
tasks ahead are not insurmountable.

nership" racial policy for the

DAMASCUS, Syria, Feb. Is
(AP President Camel Abdel
Nasser arrived yesterday for a
personal examination of the
troubled frontier between Israel
and the Syrian region of his
United Arab Republic.


In the last three weeks Israeli
and Syrian troops have clashed
several times across the border
which stretches 70 miles among
biblical sites-the Jordan River
valley northward from the Sea
Of Galilee.


This is where an uneasy
truce has prevailed between
Arabs and Jews for more than
a decade since the Palestine
war.


Nine lives have been taken
and IA persons wounded in the
recent series of clashes. For
the moment, United Nations
observers in their white tagged
jeeps are keeping the two sides
quiet.


With last Fridays clash in
so-called Zone B, fighting has
now erupted in all three de-
militarized zones established
under the 1949 armistice.


When actual fighting halted
in 1949, these areas beyond the
frontiers of Syria were held
by Syrian troops.


Israel claims these three
areas are legally part of Israel
under Israeli sovereignty. They
are part of old Palestine. The
Arabs insist the 1949 armistice
held sovereignty over these
areas in allegiance and placed
them under U. N. supervision
pending final settlement.

LONDON (AP). The
British Medical Journal
today reported the unique
case. of the middle-aged
housewife who drank to-
mato juice when she was
depressed and turned the
color of a ripe tomato.


The woman, whose name
was not disclosed, told the
doctors tomato juice was
the only thing that cheered
her up. She said she drank
312 pints a day.


A microscopic examina-
ton of her blood disclosed
two chemicals in roughly
the same proportion that
are found in her favorite
drink: Carotene, which
gives carrots their color,
and lycopene, which puts
red in tomatoes.


The woman underwent a
kidney operation and was
told to lay off the tomato
juice. Now she's back to
her normal color.

what and called for an end to

Gratis maintained control.


Final returns from yester.
days election increased the
Socialists strength from 8 to
is. Mr.. Adenauer's party lost
ground, % to 10.

test of the new Socialist plat
form, which shed the last rem
nantS of Marxist doctrine and
stressed ownership Of private
property and West German
loyalty to NATO.

showing as encouraging for
next years national election, in
which they will pit West Ber-
Inns Mayor Willy Brandt
against Mr.. Adenauer.

servers said local issues and
unique political alignments in
the Saar robbed the election

The industrial Saar, formerly
French, is West Germany's
newest state. Economic inte-
grafton into West Germany,
completed only a year ago,
brought some hardships, es-
pecially for those who lost the
more generous French social Sc
curity benefits.


Socialist vote gains were made
mostly at the expense Of smaller
parties, such as the Saar Dem
ocrats and the Communist
Party, now outlawed.


Mr.. Brandt campaigned for
Socialist candidates. Mr.. Ade-
nauer did not campaign be-
cause Of a bad cold.

With rockets chasing the moon, de-

plying increasingly crowded skies, their

pendent society is upon the photographer.

ance.

of land features from air photographs;
photographic design and the bordering
fields of navigation, geophysics, geog-
raphy and oceanography.

optical instruments demands ground
ing in physics and electronics The car
tographer must also study astronomy
mathematics and statistics and their ap-
plication to precise surveys. He must
understand the uses of maps and charts,

A portion of a wrecked oil

lanie Fair to a Belgian yard for
scrapping.

dio communication with other
ships while they awaited the
Melanie Fairs return.

However, when the Melanie
Fair returned two days ago,
the African Queen had drifted
away. The Coast Guard i'm
mediately launched a search.


After the African Queen was
found, the Melanie Fair planned
to tow it to Belgium.

Attorney General Rogers and Chief
Justice Warren used justif1ably strong
language in deploring the failure of
Congress so far to provide more judges
for the overworked Federal courts. Mr..
Rogers told the Judicial Conference that
the continued delay in authorizing more
judges-including two additional judges
for the Districts Juvenile Courts a
"Senseless kind of performance" The
Chief Justice expressed doubt that the
courts ever will be given enough judges
to meet our needs"


There have been political overtones
to congressional consideration of re-
peated administration requests for more
judges. The conference was reminded
that the number of men on the Federal
bench has remained virtually stationary
for the past seven years, despite a steady
increase in docket loads in nearly all of
the courts. The situation in the New
York Federal courts is particularly
critical. Recognizing the political as
poets of the problem, President Eisen-
hover has promised to divide the new
judgeships equally between the two
parties Mr.. Rogers told the conference
that this policy will apply also to the
new extra judges sought for the over
loaded Juvenile Court here. Moreover,
the administration has offered to defer
all appointments until after the presi-
Dental election


That promise ought to remove the
judgeships from the political arena
but still the legislation to create at least
As additional Federal judgeships and two
additional Juvenile Court judges here
languishes in committees. And while
Congress drags its feet, justice in many
courts marks time or barely creeps
ahead.

BERLIN, Sept. II (AP).-
The Soviet Air Force had an
other busy day over East Ger
many today.


Dozens of Communist MIG
fighters left white vapor trails
in the blue sky over Berlin.


Western airline pilots flying
in from West Germany re-
ported seeing more Red Jets
in the air this week than for
a long time. Allied officials
said there was no interference
with Western air traffic along
the three air corridors to the
isolated city, however.


Both the Soviet comman-
dant in East Berlin and the
Communist regime of East
Germany have threatened
vaguely that the West must
bear the consequences" If the
air corridors are "misused to
bring revenge seekers and mil
itarists to Berlin" But Allied
officials said they had no rea-
son to see anything sinister in
the current activities of the
Red air force.


Speculation among Allied
airmen was that the Red all
force is using the unusually
fine weather to make up train
ing time lost during the wet
and cloudy summer.

Head and Sheriff Paul G. Levie.

mother, father and two broth

house where the three bodies
were found last Sunday. The
houses are in a rural area out
side this small Northeast Ala
bama town.


The boys mother, Mrs. Mar
vim Brown, discovered the
bodies when she went to visit
her mother. She and the boys
father were hospitalized last
night for treatment of shock.

great-grandmother, Mrs. Ever
lena Ogle, 80, and his aunt
Mrs. John d. Martin, 81.

the ramiflcations, questions

ference started.


Will Coordinate Views


Asked if the Eisenhower
Macmillan talks were aimed at
co-ordinating an allied position
on the latest Russian proposals,
Mr.. Hagerty said. "Of course. 4"


The President and his top
diplomatic and nuclear advisers
have been giving serious study
and consideration" to the So
Wet proposals all week., appar-
emily without reaching any
definite conclusion as to how
to respond.


The SovietS moved much

week end toward accepting
American proposals to ban most
nuclear tests under a system
of inspection and control, but
leaving for further negotiation
the question of banning smaller
underground tests believed not

present methods.

The Senate last night broke


off the civil rights debate until


noon tomorrow after the South


ern filibuster produced the


longest continuous session in


the upper houses history.


The marathon Senate session on
civil rights began last Monday.
The 24-hour-a-day routine was
designed to wear down the small
band of Southern oppositionists
and bring about a decisive vote
when they had talked themselves
out. The hard core of the South
counted 16, perhaps 18, Senators.
That meant 80 pro-civil rights
Senators in the majority.


But as Bobbie Burns admon-
ished, the best laid plans some
times go awry. The filibuSter was
not 48 hours old when it became
apparent that the weary, ex-
hausted group was going to be the
majority, not the Southerners.


This was easy to understand,
the way the drama unfolded. The
Southerners, with their platoon
system, assigned four of their
group to a six-hour stint Of duty
each day while the others faded
out of sight to husband their
strength with proper sleep and
meals.


This latter was a luxury the
majority could not afford. The
Southerners did not wait until
they thought they could catch
the pro-civil rights group below
the minimum strength needed for
a quorum and thus win recess.


They demanded quorum calls
about three times in the early
morning hours. spaced sufficiently
far apart to make sleep dream
for their opponents.


AS the debate droned on during
the week and the Southerners-to
the surprise of many-kept their
speeches germane, the first ink
lings of a possible compromise
filtered through.


The activity of major impor-
tance was not going on in the
center stage, the Senate floor.
That was the place for the sound
and fury. The meetings signifying
something were being held in vari-
GUS Offices in the Capitol and Sem
ate Office buildings.

SANTIAGO, Chile, May 80
(AP) New earth tremors over
the week end battered Concep-

victims of the quakeS which
devastated southern Chile.


Today was the 10th day OF
horror for the battered nation


Thousands fed in panic when
nine more earth shocks hit Con-

Saturday night. There was no
report of new casualties, but
the city already was mourning
III persons killed last week.


The modern city of 100 900,
completely rebuilt after a dev-
astating earthquake in 1899.

Ernesto Rodriguez, editor of

Patria, said the weekend trcm-

lier shocks just crumbled."


Fear of being trapped in

residents rushing into the
streets and parks where they
huddled in terror.


Oficials predicted the death
toll in the onslaught of quakes
and tidal waves would reach
5000, with property damage
estimated at nearly 81 billion.


The latest tremors came as
southern Chile began a slow,
agonizing recovery from a
week-long onslaught of quakeS
and tidal waves. Many officials
said the recovery would take
years, perhaps decades.


Relief Supplies Rushed


Worldwide relief agencies
were rushing doctors, nurses
and tons of food, clothing and
medical equipment to Chile for
the victims.


There were fears of epidem-
les from contaminated water
supplies in some areas. Thou
sands of the homeless were re-
ported living on beaches and
under cliffs along the battered
coast.

been flown to distribution
points from the United States
Canada and various Latin
American countries. United

ing in seven field hospitals.

ago, was among the hardest

homes, the city'S hospital, bank
and two major hotels were de-

The United States atomic
submarine Sarge has smashed
through the ice at the North
Pole and planted the flag of
Hawaii-her home State-at
the top of the world.


The Navy said late yesterday
the sub broke through the
North pole ice Tuesday after
noon and then resumed her
cruise in the Arctic Oceans
great basin.


The Sarge had been preceded
to the pole by two sister nu-
clear subs, the Nautilus and
the Skate. The Nautilus reached
the pole on August 8, 1858. The
Skate made its first trip on
August IL. 1858. then repeated
her cruise last March.


The Sargo's journey during
the Arctic winter again empha-
sized the power of American
nuclear submarines to prowl
the international waters above
Rusiia in any season.


The Navy said the Sarge is
collecting oceanographic data,
including data on the ocean
bottom and the Arctic ice,


The Sarge slipped out Of
Pearl Harbor, her home port,
on January 18. In her ex-
plorations she Travelled a longer
course than the direct 4,200
nautical miles from her base
to the pole.


After submerging at the edge
of the Arctic ice pack in the
Bering Sea southwest of Alaska,
she was under the ice for 2,744
miles before reaching the pole
IA days and 81 hours later.


She pushed through the ice
seven times during the two
weeks. The last two times she
penetrated ice about 3-feet
thick. which was the minimum
thickness she found. Only the
high coming tower of the sub
marine was showed up through
the ice on the last two break
throughs.


The Hawaiian flag was
planted at the pole by L..
Comdr. John H. Nicholson, the
Sargo's skipper.


The tops of the nuclear sub
marines are reinforced to per-
NIT ice breakthroughs. An up
ward drive pushes them through
the ice in their normal cruising
position. No boring or ramming
Is involved.

New public housing in the District
has been blocked for long time by the
difficulty in finding feasible sites. Now,
however, this problem has been brought
to the critical stage by warning that
the Federal Government will withdraw
the authority to build new public hous-
ing here unless specific sites for some
1,400 units are found by June 80.


The new units, of course, are needed.
Most of the eligible low-income families
displaced from Southwest redevelopment
areas fortunately have been placed in
projects. But other families who need
public housing soon will be moved from
Northwest renewal areas, and still others
constantly are being displaced by houS-
ing code enforcement and other city
programs. Entirely apart from dis
places, moreover, some 4,500 families
already are on the waiting lists of the
National Capital Housing Authority.


The FHA'S June 80 ultimatum is
hardly surprising. The new Washington
projects were authorized in 1856, and
four years is long time for them to
hang fire without progress. In another
sense, however, the deadline may turn
out to be blessing, for there has been
a good bit of dillydallying about the
site question among the various agencies
involved. Now that the pressure is on,
we hope that National Capital Planning
Commission and District officials will
join the NCHA in a firm determination
that there are or that there are not
appropriate sites for public housing still
available in Washington.

CATANIA, Sicily. July 10
(AP). - Molten lava flowed
down the slopes of Mount Etna
today, but the rumble and ex-
plosions that accompanied the
eruption subsidized at least
temporarily.


Etna, Europe's highest ac-
tive volcano, erupted again
yesterday. sending a mush-
room-like cloud miles into the
air, obscuring the sun and
causing panic both on the
island of Sicily and on the
Italian mainland.


The blast was the most
powerful in many years and
reminded old-timers of the
1908 eruption and earthquake
which destroyed Messina.


The blast ripped out a new
crater on the east or Ionic Sea
side of the 10,705-foot volcano.
From the central crater came
massive, molten blocks of
stone and ashes.


The ashes were scattered by
wind as far as Taormina. the
resort town. and beyond to Reg
gio Calabria, on the Italian
mainland. Ships at sea, cov-
cred by the ashes, radioed here
for information. Stones we're
blasted as far as Piedimonte
Etneo. 20 miles from the crater
and damaged parked automo-
biles.


Some small forest fires were
started. However, there still
was no imminent danger to
villages and farm fields far
down on the volcano.


Catania's Volcano Institute,
which maintains a constant
check on Etna's activity, said
that the explosions had ceased
but that the lava flow con-
tinued, This was flowing slowly
down the Valley of the Lion,
following ancient lava beds.


Observers said that the ac-
tivity of the central crater
something which had not hap
pened since 1928-indicated
that the mass of lava had
risen high in the volcano.
